items.title: 0.11.9 release missing GitHub Artifact Attestations
items.body:
## Disclaimer
This summary was created by AI. I validated that the findings were correct.
## Summary
The `0.11.9` release artifacts are missing GitHub Artifact Attestations (SLSA provenance). This causes tools that verify attestations before installing (e.g., [mise](https://github.com/jdx/mise)) to fail when attempting to install `uv@0.11.9`.
The [release notes](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/releases/tag/0.11.9) mention:
> Note due to a timeout publishing to crates.io, the GitHub portion of this release was published manually by a maintainer using the artifacts built in CI.

This manual publish appears to have skipped the attestation generation step.
## Reproduction
### Verify 0.11.9 (fails)
```bash
$ gh release download 0.11.9 --repo astral-sh/uv --pattern "uv-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz" --dir /tmp/uv-test
$ gh attestation verify /tmp/uv-test/uv-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz --repo astral-sh/uv
Error: HTTP 404: Not Found (https://api.github.com/repos/astral-sh/uv/attestations/sha256:ac3e5051edbf30613b0f90d1c18d4807fea6b246f37490799fee0c1284a658b2?per_page=30&predicate_type=https://slsa.dev/provenance/v1)
```
### Verify 0.11.8 (succeeds)
```bash
$ gh release download 0.11.8 --repo astral-sh/uv --pattern "uv-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz" --dir /tmp/uv-test-8
$ gh attestation verify /tmp/uv-test-8/uv-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz --repo astral-sh/uv
# (exits 0, no output — verification successful)
```
## Impact
Tools that rely on GitHub Artifact Attestations for supply-chain verification cannot install `uv@0.11.9`. For example, [mise](https://github.com/jdx/mise) (which uses the `aqua` backend to install `uv`) fails with:
```
mise ERROR Failed to install aqua:astral-sh/uv@latest: GitHub artifact attestations verification failed:
Verification failed: Workflow verification failed: expected 'astral-sh/uv/.github/workflows/release.yml',
found certificate: None, provenance: None
```
This breaks CI pipelines that use `mise` to install `uv` without pinning to a specific version (i.e., using `uv@latest`).
## Expected behavior
All release artifacts should have GitHub Artifact Attestations attached, as documented in the release notes' "Verifying GitHub Artifact Attestations" section.
## Suggested fix
Either:
1. Re-publish the attestations for the existing 0.11.9 artifacts (if possible), or
2. Document this as a known limitation of the 0.11.9 release and recommend pinning to 0.11.8 until 0.11.10 is released through the standard CI pipeline.

items.title: Unable to use system-installed PyGObject (GTK) in uv venv, causing matplotlib to fall back to non-interactive backend

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or improvement to existing functionality

items.body:
### Summary

When using a virtual environment created by `uv venv` (without `--system-site-packages`), Python cannot import the `gi` module even though the necessary system package (`python-gobject`) is fully installed via the system package manager (Arch Linux, `pacman`). This causes matplotlib to fall back to the non-interactive `Agg` backend, preventing any plot windows from appearing.

The core issue is that standard virtual environments isolate from system site‑packages. While this is correct for pure Python packages, it breaks commonly used GUI libraries (GTK, Qt, Tk) that are often installed at the system level.

Current workarounds (`--system-site-packages`, manually compiling `PyGObject` in every project, `.pth` files) are fragile, non‑portable, or destroy environment isolation. A native `uv` mechanism to handle system‑level GUI dependencies would greatly improve the user experience for the many developers and scientists who rely on interactive plotting on Linux.

Desired solutions could include:
- A way to automatically detect and expose system packages required for common GUI backends.
- A built‑in hook or plugin system (similar to `virtualenvwrapper`'s `postmkvirtualenv`) allowing users to run custom steps after venv creation.
- A command‑line flag to include specific system packages (more granular than `--system-site-packages`).
- Official documentation or a recipe that solves the “matplotlib + GTK/Qt on Linux” problem once and for all.

### Example

## Current behavior (broken)

$ pacman -Q python-gobject
python-gobject 3.56.2-1

$ uv venv
$ source .venv/bin/activate
$ uv pip install matplotlib

$ python -c "import gi"
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 1, in <module>
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'gi'

$ python -c "import matplotlib; print(matplotlib.get_backend())"
agg

## Desired behavior

After a hypothetical `uv` command like `uv venv --with-system-gui` (or an equivalent hook), the same setup would work out of the box:

$ uv venv --with-system-gui   # or similar mechanism
$ source .venv/bin/activate
$ uv pip install matplotlib

$ python -c "import gi; print('gi loaded successfully')"
gi loaded successfully

$ python -c "import matplotlib; print(matplotlib.get_backend())"
GTK3Agg   # or any interactive backend

This would allow interactive matplotlib plots to appear immediately, without additional manual steps.

items.title: `[tool.uv.build-backend.data]` files are not installed in editable mode
items.body:
### Summary

Files declared in `[tool.uv.build-backend.data]` are correctly packaged into the wheel by `uv build`, and a non-editable `uv pip install <wheel>` correctly copies them to the right destination (e.g., the `purelib` slot lands at site-packages root, `scripts` at the venv's `bin/`).

But an editable install (`uv pip install -e .`) silently skips them: no data files land, no warning. The dropped files are gone in editable mode whether they're `.pth` files, binaries, configs, etc.

```toml
# pyproject.toml
[build-system]
build-backend = "uv_build"
requires = ["uv_build>=0.11,<0.12"]

[project]
name = "mypkg"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.12"

[tool.uv.build-backend.data]
purelib = "data"
```

Layout:

```tree
uv-bug/
├── pyproject.toml
├── data/
│   └── mypkg-startup.pth
└── src/
    └── mypkg/
        └── __init__.py
```

Commands

```bash
mkdir uv-bug && cd uv-bug && uv venv
mkdir -p src/mypkg data && touch src/mypkg/__init__.py
echo 'import sys; print("[pth] fired", file=sys.stderr)' > data/mypkg-startup.pth
# Save the `pyproject.toml` block shown above as `uv-bug/pyproject.toml`.
export VIRTUAL_ENV="$PWD/.venv"  # so `uv pip install` targets this venv

# editable install: silent
# .pth never lands at site-packages root, doesn't fire
uv pip install -e .
.venv/bin/python -c ''

# non-editable install: .pth lands at site-packages root, fires on every startup
uv build --wheel
uv pip install --force-reinstall dist/*.whl
.venv/bin/python -c ''   # → "[pth] fired"
```

`<name>-<version>.data/` is the canonical way to ship arbitrary files alongside a Python package. With editable installs silently dropping them, development of any such project has a gap from production behavior in and editable dev setup.

### Additional context

[PEP 660](https://peps.python.org/pep-0660/) states that editable installs should match the regular-install behavior:

> When a project is installed in editable mode, users expect the installation to behave identically as a regular installation.

So `uv pip install -e .` silently dropping a `[tool.uv.build-backend.data]` can also be considered a divergence there.

For reference, Hatchling does not have this issue, one can use `tool.hatch.build.targets.wheel.force-include`.

```toml
# pyproject.toml
[build-system]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"
requires = ["hatchling"]

[project]
name = "mypkg"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.12"

[tool.hatch.build.targets.wheel]
packages = ["src/mypkg"]

[tool.hatch.build.targets.wheel.force-include]
"data/mypkg-startup.pth" = "mypkg-startup.pth"
```

`uv pip install -e .` against this `pyproject.toml` lands `mypkg-startup.pth` at site-packages root, and a fresh `.venv/bin/python -c ''` fires it, matching my desired behavior.

I think it's worth extending `uv_build`'s editable hook to ship `[tool.uv.build-backend.data]` entries the same way hatchling's `force-include` does. Or at least emitting a warning when a data file is silently skipped in editable mode.

### Platform

Darwin 25.3.0 arm64

### Version

uv 0.11.8 (Homebrew 2026-04-27 aarch64-apple-darwin)

### Python version

Python 3.12.8

items.title: `exclude-newer-package` silently ignored by `uv pip compile` when combined with global `exclude-newer`
items.body:
### Summary

First of all, thank you for contributing this amazing tool to the community. 

The [documentation](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/reference/settings/#exclude-newer-package) mentions that a global `exclude-newer` setting can be overwritten by using package specific `exclude-newer-package` settings. 

> Set a package to false to exempt it from the global [exclude-newer](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/reference/settings/#exclude-newer) constraint entirely.

This does not seem to work with `uv pip compile`

```sh
# create minimal requirements file with frequently updated package
printf "boto3" > req.in

# create config file 1 - global exclude-newer
printf 'exclude-newer = "7 days"\n' > config1.toml

# create config file 2 - global exclude-newer and then per-package overwrite
printf 'exclude-newer = "7 days"\nexclude-newer-package = { "boto3" = false }\n' > config2.toml

# compile environment
uv pip compile req.in 
# boto3==1.43.2

uv pip compile req.in --config-file config1.toml
# boto3==1.42.96

uv pip compile req.in --config-file config2.toml
# would have expected boto3==1.43.2, found boto3==1.42.96
```

I am not sure if I am misunderstanding how `--exclude-newer-package` works or in which context it works, but I expected the package level overwrite to work in the `config2.toml` examples

---

This behavior is consistent when using the CLI flags instead of a config file - although it seems the `uv pip compile` documentation does not explicitly mention the per-package-reset of global `exclude-newer` AFAICT. 

```sh
echo "boto3" > req.in

uv pip compile req.in --no-config -U
uv pip compile req.in --no-config -U  --exclude-newer "7 days"
uv pip compile req.in --no-config -U  --exclude-newer "7 days" --exclude-newer-package "boto3=false"
```

### Platform

Darwin 25.3.0 arm64

### Version

uv 0.11.8 (0e961dd9a 2026-04-27 aarch64-apple-darwin)

### Python version

Python 3.12.11

items.title: `[dependency-groups]` entry `pkg[extra]` stops activating `extra` once `[tool.uv.conflicts]` lists it
items.body:
### Summary

When `[dependency-groups]` contains an entry that references a self-extra (`pkg[foo]`), and that same extra is listed in `[tool.uv.conflicts]`, activating the dependency group no longer activates the extra. This makes `uv sync` (which activates default groups) and `uv sync --extra foo` diverge, even though the group is defined as `foo = ["pkg[foo]"]`.

When a `[dependency-groups]` entry references a self-extra (`pkg[foo]`) and that extra is listed in `[tool.uv.conflicts]`, `uv sync` no longer activates the extra through the default-group path. `uv sync --extra foo` works correctly, but bare `uv sync` silently drops the extra's entire dependency subtree (even though the group is defined as `foo = ["pkg[foo]"]` and is normally equivalent to `--extra foo`).
  
```toml
[dependency-groups]
dev = ["demo[dev]"]

[project]
name = "demo"
version = "0"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies = []

[project.optional-dependencies]
train = ["skyrl[skyrl-train]"]
summarize = ["vllm"]
dev = ["demo[train]"]

[tool.uv]
conflicts = [
  [{extra = "dev"}, {extra = "summarize"}],
  [{extra = "summarize"}, {extra = "train"}]
]

[tool.uv.sources]
skyrl = {git = "https://github.com/NovaSky-AI/SkyRL.git"}
```

Here's CLI usage showing the bug:

```console
$ uv lock
Resolved 230 packages in 1.13s

$ rm -rf .venv && uv sync --frozen
Using CPython 3.13.2
Creating virtual environment at: .venv
Checked in 0.00ms
# 0 packages installed

$ rm -rf .venv && uv sync --frozen --extra dev
# 112 packages installed, including skyrl, skyrl-gym, accelerate, tensordict, wandb, torchdata, ...
```

`uv.lock` contains:

```toml
[package.dev-dependencies]
dev = [
    { name = "demo" },
    { name = "demo", extra = ["dev"], marker = "extra == 'extra-4-demo-dev' or (extra == 'extra-4-demo-summarize' and extra == 'extra-4-demo-train')" },
]
```

The `demo[dev]` reference is gated behind the synthetic conflict-group key `extra == 'extra-4-demo-dev'`. Activating the `dev` dependency group does not set this key (only `--extra dev` does), so the extra's contents (`demo[train]` → `skyrl[skyrl-train]` → 112 transitive packages) are filtered out during sync.

I expect `uv sync` and `uv sync --extra dev` to produce identical environments, since `[dependency-groups] dev = ["demo[dev]"]` is defined as "install `demo` with its `dev` extra." Notably, without `[tool.uv.conflicts]`, the two invocations are identical; adding `conflicts` silently breaks the equivalence.

Here's some issues with a possibly related underlying mechanism:

- https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/13073
- https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/13070

### Platform

Darwin 25.3.0 arm64

### Version

uv 0.11.7 (9d177269e 2026-04-15 aarch64-apple-darwin)

### Python version

Python 3.13.2

labels.name: great writeup

items.body:
### Summary

I just discovered #19022 while subscribed to #18708, and it looks like a great improvement to eliminate timestamp noise.

In the same spirit of this workaround, I just wonder if we could use the sane no-op flag for `[options.exclude-newer-package]`.

See how a package configured with a relative span (like `0 day`), the lockfile records the a full timestamp:

```toml
[options]
exclude-newer = "0001-01-01T00:00:00Z" # no-op placeholder (fixed by #19022)
exclude-newer-span = "P1W"

[options.exclude-newer-package]
mypackage = { timestamp = "2026-04-21T14:32:07.819274Z", span = "PT0S" }  # still changes every run
```

So currently every `uv lock` invokation update the `timestamp`.

### Example

Configuration in `pyproject.toml`:

```toml
[tool.uv]
exclude-newer = "1 week"
exclude-newer-package = { mypackage = "0 day" }
```

Running `uv lock` twice in quick succession produces a diff:

```diff
 [options.exclude-newer-package]
-mypackage = { timestamp = "2026-04-21T14:32:07.819274Z", span = "PT0S" }
+mypackage = { timestamp = "2026-04-21T14:32:09.123456Z", span = "PT0S" }
```

My proposal is to reuse the same no-op placeholder when a span is present:

```toml
[options.exclude-newer-package]
mypackage = { timestamp = "0001-01-01T00:00:00Z", span = "PT0S" }
```

This would make the lockfile fully stable across runs.

```
  ╰─▶ Package `my-util` was included as a URL dependency. URL dependencies must be expressed as direct requirements or
      constraints. Consider adding `my-util @ file:///home/user/uv-testing/my-workspace/my-util` to your dependencies
      or constraints file.
```

I cannot tell whether this is a bug or something that is covered by https://docs.astral.sh/uv/reference/internals/resolver/#url-dependencies. To me, it seems as though depending on workspace packages doesn't count as an "index package" and isn't subject to the same issues that resolving index packages have (since we directly list `workspace = true` as the source of the package). Since neither `my-util` nor `my-backend` is included as a dependency in `my-tool`'s wheel, it seems wrong to enforce these resolution requirements onto building.

The docs state, 

> uv requires that URLs are either declared directly ... or by other URL dependencies.

In the error it seems as though my-backend is attempting to be resolved as a URL dependency (I guess something happens in uv which takes a workspace package and transforms it to a URL dependency) and hence it should be OK for it to include other url dependencies.

### Reproducible Pyprojects

The pyproject's for the example are as follows:

**my-workspace/pyproject.toml**
```toml
[project]
name = "my-workspace"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Add your description here"
readme = "README.md"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies = []

[tool.uv]
package = false

[tool.uv.workspace]
members = ["my-util", "my-backend", "my-tool"]

[tool.uv.sources]
my-backend = { workspace = true }
my-util = { workspace = true }
```

**my-workspace/my-util/pyproject.toml**
```toml
[project]
name = "my-util"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Add your description here"
readme = "README.md"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies = []
```

**my-workspace/my-backend/pyproject.toml**
```toml
[project]
name = "my-backend"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Add your description here"
readme = "README.md"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies = ["my-util"]
```

**my-workspace/my-tool/pyproject.toml**
```toml
[project]
name = "my-tool"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Add your description here"
readme = "README.md"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies = []

[build-system]
requires = ["my-backend", "setuptools"] # note setuptools is included here since I didn't actually make a real backend for this example, but it should be irrelevant to this issue
```

### Workarounds

The most succinct workaround is to have `my-tool` declare `my-util` as a build-dependency. I.e.

**my-workspace/my-tool/pyproject.toml**
```toml
[project]
name = "my-tool"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Add your description here"
readme = "README.md"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies = []

[build-system]
requires = ["my-backend", "setuptools", "my-util"] 
```

In my circumstance, I have a really large workspace with 100s of workspace packages which all depend on `my-backend` or equivalent sort of packages (i.e. plugins). These plugins can be changed often and their dependencies on other local workspace packages can also be changed. It is a pain to go through every dependent workspace package to update their build dependencies with the new transitive dependencies that are necessary for the build plugins it wants to use. There should be no need to have to update transitive dependencies.

These are some other workarounds I've started using that don't involve constantly updating workspace packages with transitive dependencies.

For `uv build` commands specifically, my workaround is using a build-constraints file like this:
```
echo "my-util @ file:///home/user/uv-testing/my-workspace/my-util" > my-constraints.txt
uv build --wheel --build-constraints my-constraints.txt --package my-tool
```
Essentially just have all the common util-like packages that build plugins depend on in a constraints file and use that constraints file for every package you build.

In cases where `uv sync` requires actually calling the backend of affected files, it also fails. For example, let's include `my-tool` into a dependency group so that it'll sync when we sync the root project.

**my-workspace/pyproject.toml**
```toml
[project]
name = "my-workspace"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Add your description here"
readme = "README.md"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies = []

[tool.uv]
package = false

[tool.uv.workspace]
members = ["my-util", "my-backend", "my-tool"]

[dependency-groups]
tools = ["my-tool"]

[tool.uv.sources]
my-tool = { workspace = true }
my-backend = { workspace = true }
my-util = { workspace = true }
```

```
$ uv sync --group tools
Resolved 4 packages in 2ms
  × Failed to build `my-tool @ file:///home/user/uv-testing/my-workspace/my-tool`
  ├─▶ Failed to resolve requirements from `build-system.requires`
  ├─▶ No solution found when resolving: `setuptools`, `my-backend @
  │   file:///home/user/uv-testing/my-workspace/my-backend`
  ├─▶ Failed to resolve dependencies for package `my-backend==0.1.0`
  ╰─▶ Package `my-util` was included as a URL dependency. URL dependencies must be expressed as direct requirements or
      constraints. Consider adding `my-util @ file:///home/user/uv-testing/my-workspace/my-util` to your dependencies
      or constraints file.
  help: `my-tool` was included because `my-workspace:tools` (v0.1.0) depends on `my-tool`
```

My workaround for this is using `build-constraint-dependencies`. It seems like this ends up resolving `my-util` prior to the build-system getting mad that `my-backend` is using a URL dependency.
```
[tool.uv]
build-constraint-dependencies = ["my-util"]
```

items.title: uv constantly warns about empty `SSL_CERT_DIR`
items.body:
### Summary

With the 0.11.X release of uv, there are constant warnings about an empty `SSL_CERT_DIR`.

Reproduce with conda:
1. conda create -n uv_bug python=3.14 -y
2. conda activate uv_bug
3. pip install "uv>=0.11"
4. uv pip install numpy

This will yield: `warning: Ignoring `SSL_CERT_DIR`. No certificates found in:` which will also show up with other uv commands.

The problem is that conda by default creates an activation script for openssl in the environment (e.g., in `%userprofile%\miniforge3\envs\pref\etc\conda\activate.d`) with the following content:
```powershell
if (-not $Env:SSL_CERT_FILE) {
    $Env:SSL_CERT_FILE = "$Env:CONDA_PREFIX\Library\ssl\cacert.pem"
    $Env:__CONDA_OPENSSL_CERT_FILE_SET = "1"
}
if (-not $Env:SSL_CERT_DIR) {
    $Env:SSL_CERT_DIR = "$Env:CONDA_PREFIX\Library\ssl\certs"
    $Env:__CONDA_OPENSSL_CERT_DIR_SET = "1"
}
```

By default, `$Env:CONDA_PREFIX\Library\ssl\cacert.pem` points to an existing file but `$Env:CONDA_PREFIX\Library\ssl\certs` is empty (strictly speaking it only contains a `.keep` file). The latter is causing the warning message. One could argue that conda should not point `SSL_CERT_DIR` to an empty directory but I also think that uv should not warn about this if `SSL_CERT_FILE` points already to an existing file.

uv 0.10.X did not have this warning. Unfortunately, this warning is emitted with every uv command.

### Platform

Windows 11

### Version

0.11.6

### Python version

3.14.4

items.title: Feature request: advisory-aware exclude-newer that exempts CVE fixes from the cooldown window
items.body:
## Motivation

A concrete, reproducible scenario that happens on every CVE disclosure whose fix lands inside the `exclude-newer` window:

1. `uv lock --upgrade` runs in CI, respects `exclude-newer`.
2. A CVE is disclosed on package `X`. Maintainers publish fix `X+1` the same day.
3. The resolver refuses to see `X+1` because it is inside the cooldown window.
4. `pip-audit` (or any live-DB scanner) queries the advisory database and flags the pinned vulnerable version.
5. CI goes red.
6. There is no version constraint the user can write to escape this: `exclude-newer` is a hard pre-filter on the catalog, so constraints like `cryptography >= 46.0.7` produce `No solution found when resolving dependencies`.
7. The only way to clear CI is to wait for the window to expire, or remove `exclude-newer` from the project.

This is a structural conflict between two policies that are individually reasonable but logically incompatible when layered: "hide new versions for N days" and "check against a live advisory database". It recurs on every future CVE that ships inside the window.

## Proposal

Add an opt-in mode to `exclude-newer` that exempts any version whose advisory-DB entry indicates it fixes a known vulnerability. The policy would read: *hide fresh releases, unless the fresh release is a security patch.*

Possible config shape:

```toml
[tool.uv]
exclude-newer = { days = 8, exempt-vulnerability-fixes = true }
```

Implementation could consult PyPI's advisory DB, OSV (osv.dev), or GitHub Security Advisories. At resolve time, for each candidate version inside the cooldown window, check whether it is listed as a fix for a known advisory. If yes, allow the resolver to see it.

## Why this matters

The current flat `exclude-newer` is the only form of cooldown whose failure mode is a guaranteed CVE-exposure extension. The proposed advisory-aware variant removes that failure mode while preserving the supply-chain benefit of the window for all non-security releases.

## Alternatives considered

- **`exclude-newer-package` allow-lists**: require manual per-package maintenance, accumulate indefinitely, cannot anticipate which package will be hit next.
- **Removing `exclude-newer` entirely**: trades the cooldown benefit for a different set of failure modes.
- **Shorter cooldown window**: does not eliminate the deadlock, just shortens how long CI stays red.

## Background

I wrote a first-principles analysis of why flat pre-resolver cooldowns are dominated by buffering later in the pipeline, including a Monte Carlo cost model that puts the break-even risk ratio for an 8-day cooldown at roughly 12,000 for a typical non-financial-critical service:

https://alexsavio.github.io/dependency-cooldown-considered-harmful.html

The post explicitly calls out advisory-aware cooldown as the constructive ask for uv. I am opening this issue to follow through on that ask.

I am not asking for `exclude-newer` to be removed or deprecated. Only for an opt-in variant that breaks the deadlock.

osxphotos uses mutually exclusive platform_release markers:
```toml

pyobjc-framework-AVFoundation>=10.0;      platform_release >= '22.0'
```
On macOS 26.4, platform_release is approximately 25.x. The string comparison '25.x' >= '22.0' is True, so the second branch should be selected.
uv appears to either:

- Be performing universal (cross-platform) resolution and taking the lowest common version across both branches, or
- Mishandling the platform_release string comparison for two-digit Darwin kernel versions (e.g. 25.x vs 22.x)

Adding an explicit override resolves the issue:
```toml
[tool.uv]
override-dependencies = [
    "pyobjc-framework-avfoundation>=12.0",
]
```
### Additional Context

Python 3.13 dropped pkg_resources from the stdlib, so this also surfaces as a secondary build failure — but the real fix is selecting the correct version branch.
This may affect all pyobjc-framework-* packages that use the same platform_release gating pattern.

uv 0.11.6 (Homebrew 2026-04-09 aarch64-apple-darwin)

### Python version

Python 3.14.4, but same error with Python 3.13

items.title: Provide a clean “version-only” output option for uv python list

labels.name: enhancement

items.body:
### Summary

Currently, uv python list outputs detailed information about installed Python distributions, including full identifiers and platform-specific metadata, for example:
```
cpython-3.14.3-windows-x86_64-none  C:\Users\...\python.exe
```
While this is useful for debugging and environment inspection, it becomes noisy when the user only wants to know which Python versions are installed.

There is currently no built-in option to display only the installed Python versions in a clean and minimal format.

It would be useful to have a dedicated flag or output format that returns only version numbers (e.g. 3.11.7, 3.14.3) without implementation details, architecture strings, or file paths.

### Example

### Current behavior

```bash
uv python list --only-installed
```

Output:

```
cpython-3.14.3-windows-x86_64-none  C:\Users\...\python.exe
cpython-3.11.7-windows-x86_64-none  C:\Users\...\python.exe
```

---

### Proposed behavior

A new flag such as:

```bash
uv python list --versions-only
```

or:

```bash
uv python list --format version
```

would output:

```
3.11.7
3.14.3
```

---

### Benefit

* Cleaner CLI output for humans
* Easier parsing for scripts and automation
* Avoids the need for regex filtering or external processing
* Improves usability for version selection workflows

### Summary

First I create a config file specifying a default cooldown period of 1w:

```toml
[pip]

```

Then create and activate a test venv:

```sh
uv venv ~/python/venvs/cooldown_test
source python/venvs/cooldown_test/bin/activate
```

Now install a package (that I know has a recent update):

```sh
uv pip install cryptography
```

Works as expected, giving me the slightly dated `cryptography==46.0.6`:

```log
Using Python 3.14.2 environment at: python/venvs/cooldown_test
Resolved 3 packages in 127ms
Installed 3 packages in 11ms

 + cryptography==46.0.6

```

Oh no! There's a recent CVE in that version, best grab the latest one:

```sh
uv pip install cryptography --exclude-newer=0h
```

Nothing happens ☹️ 

OK, let's try specifying a version:

```sh
uv pip install cryptography==46.0.7
```

Here's where I get the confusing message:

items.title: Only apply `exclude-newer` under dependency version constraints

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or improvement to existing functionality

items.body:
### Summary

The current behavior of `exclude-newer` makes it quite difficult to use in various scenarios:
* when there is version released fixing a critical issues, we need to update then manage a whitelist, see https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/18792
* dependency update bots need to deal with that ? or be more coupled to the package manager
* it pollutes the lock file with timestamp information

I would instead suggest this setting to only apply when `uv` pick a version and not when setting a version range. This is happening mostly on "lock" when `uv` as to decide to pick a new transitive dependency, or pick a new version of a dependency specified with a boundary (like `>=1.0`), but only there.

So if I say they want to use 1.0.2, `uv` should just comply to that, regardless the age of 1.0.2. The same, if I specify I want to use 1.0.2 and there is a min possible version of a transitive dependency that is too young, it should still use it, because it is a choice of mine.

On the contrary, if I am running `uv lock` and I delegate to uv the role to pin specific versions, I am expecting `uv` to follow the `exclude-newer` settings

### Summary

 When a workspace root's optional dependency activates a workspace member's extra (e.g. `root[cpu]` → `member[cpu]`), and the member declares a `conflicts` between its own `cpu`/`cuda` extras (to pick torch from different indices), `uv export --extra cpu` on the root does **not** include `torch` in the output.

When `uv export --extra cpu` runs, it sets the root's `cpu` extra but never the member's internal conflict-fork extra, so `member[cpu]` is never activated and `torch` is never included.

**Minimal reproduction:**

```
my-workspace/
├── pyproject.toml             # workspace root
└── packages/
    └── member/
        └── pyproject.toml     # workspace member
```

`packages/member/pyproject.toml`:
```toml

name = "member"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.13"
dependencies = []

[project.optional-dependencies]
cpu  = ["torch>=2.0.0"]
cuda = ["torch>=2.0.0"]

[tool.uv]
conflicts = [
  [{ extra = "cpu" }, { extra = "cuda" }],
]

[tool.uv.sources]
torch = [
  { index = "torch-cpu",  extra = "cpu"  },
  { index = "torch-cuda", extra = "cuda" },
]

[[tool.uv.index]]
name = "torch-cpu"
url = "https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu"

[[tool.uv.index]]

url = "https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu130"
```

```toml
members = ["packages/member"]
```

items.title: exclude-newer: allow exempting packages with no upload date
items.body:
## Problem

When using `exclude-newer` with a private PyPI registry (Sonatype Nexus), packages that lack upload timestamps are rejected even when `exclude-newer-package` is set for them.

Nexus doesn't emit upload dates in its simple API responses. Setting `exclude-newer-package = { my-pkg = "2099-01-01" }` doesn't help — uv still reports "has no publish time" and excludes the package.

## Current behavior

```
× No solution found when resolving dependencies for split (markers: python_full_version >= '3.14'):
╰─▶ Because loee-commons==0.8.0 has no publish time and there are no versions of loee-commons,
    we can conclude that loee-commons>=0.8.0,<1 cannot be used.
```

## Expected behavior

When `exclude-newer-package` is set for a package, packages with no upload date should be treated as allowed (the user has explicitly opted in to that package).

## Suggested alternatives

1. Treat "no publish date" as "always allowed" when `exclude-newer-package` is set for that package
2. Support a plain exemption list (e.g., `exclude-newer-exempt = ["my-pkg"]`) for packages that should bypass the check entirely
3. Support per-index `exclude-newer` so private indexes can be excluded from the global setting

## Workaround

Set `UV_EXCLUDE_NEWER` as a CI env var instead of in `pyproject.toml`. This works because Docker builds use `--frozen` and don't need resolution, but it means the protection isn't declarative.

### Summary

I'm trying to use uv to prevent supply chain attacks on my scripts.

I use something like this (in a `.py` file):
```
#!/usr/bin/env -S uv run --locked --script

# requires-python = "..."
# dependencies = [
...
```

I think more secure behaviour would be for `--locked` to use the contents of the lockfile, if the file is empty or not present, either fail or print a warning about an empty lockfile and just install nothing (which would almost certainly cause the python script to ultimately fail, but at least the warning would give a clue to devs what's going on).

I have tried to enable `exclude_newer` in a repo that sources packages from both PyPI and a private AWS CodeArtifact source. I am doing this to mitigate risks associated with recent supply chain attacks, I believe this is a common use of this feature.

Unfortunately because the [AWS CodeArtifact API](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codeartifact/latest/ug/python-compatibility.html) does not support the required date time publishing meta data, uv cannot resolve the dependencies. I do not need `exclude_newer` applied here because the packages in this package store are always older than my `exclude_newer` setting. I believe others will be in a similar situation. 

**Suggestion:** Allow some sources to be exempt from this setting. 



### Example


Example error I get for a CodeArtifact package when running `uv lock`
```
× No solution found when resolving dependencies for split (markers:
```

items.title: Reject locked malware installations

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or improvement to existing functionality

items.body:
If the user's `uv.lock` contains a version that is known to be malicious, then we should reject its installation. 

This is slightly different from what `uv audit` does -- `uv audit` principally checks from known vulnerabilities, not malware or compromised packages. The latter is reported via a distinct "stream" on OSV (`MAL-` reports).

I need to think a bit more about the design here/implications.

- [x] Support filtering by malware (`MAL-`) in the OSV client: https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/18934
- [x] Fetch `MAL-` entries during lockfile installation and reject the install if we have any: https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/18936
- [x] Cache `MAL-` lookups: #19038

items.title: `uv venv` recommends use of `source` in incompatible shells
items.body:
### Summary

`uv venv` suggests sourcing the virtual environment with `source` regardless of whether the current shell supports `source`. `source` is not POSIX-compliant, and not provided by many commonly available shells such as `ash` and `dash`. The POSIX-compliant instruction is `. .venv/bin/activate`.

On Ubuntu, or a system with `dash` manually installed:

```shell
$ dash
$ uv venv .venv
Using CPython 3.11.15
Creating virtual environment at: .venv
Activate with: source .venv/bin/activate
$ source .venv/bin/activate
dash: 8: source: not found
$ . .venv/bin/activate
(.venv) $ 
```

### Platform

e..g. Ubuntu, Alpine

### Version

uv 0.11.1 (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu)

### Python version

3.11 / whatever

items.body:
### Summary

## Summary

Since version 0.10.0 and last verified with 0.11.2, uv refuses to install debug wheels into a venv with a debug CPython. This appears to be a regression compared with uv 0.9.30.

In slightly more detail:
* Using uv to create a venv with a CPython debug build works.
* Using uv to build a wheel of a native package works.
* Installing a debug wheel built by uv into a project venv that uses a CPython debug build does NOT work.

## Steps to reproduce

### Preparation

Use the following tarball for a trivial native package:

[native_demo-0.1.0.tar.gz](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/26346629/native_demo-0.1.0.tar.gz)

Mount or copy this into a docker container running `ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:debian`.
Then inside the running container:
```
apt update -qq && apt install -y python3-dbg python3-dev
uv venv --python /usr/bin/python3-dbg   # Important: debug build
. .venv/bin/activate
```
So far so good.

### Action

Expected: uv can build and install the native package.

Observed: installation fails. Details:
```
# uv pip install /tmp/native_demo-0.1.0.tar.gz
Using Python 3.13.5 environment at: /root/.venv
Resolved 1 package in 20ms
      Built native-demo @ file:///tmp/native_demo-0.1.0.tar.gz
  x Failed to build `native-demo @ file:///tmp/native_demo-0.1.0.tar.gz`
  `-> The built wheel `native_demo-0.1.0-cp313-cp313d-linux_x86_64.whl` is not compatible with the current Python 3.13
      on manylinux x86_64
```

If we dig into it, we see that the wheel build succeeds, but the install fails:
```
# uv build --wheel /tmp/native_demo-0.1.0.tar.gz
[snip]
Successfully built /tmp/native_demo-0.1.0-cp313-cp313d-linux_x86_64.whl

# uv pip install /tmp/native_demo-0.1.0-cp313-cp313d-linux_x86_64.whl
Using Python 3.13.5 environment at: /root/.venv
Resolved 1 package in 15ms
error: Failed to determine installation plan
  Caused by: A path dependency is incompatible with the current platform: /tmp/native_demo-0.1.0-cp313-cp313d-linux_x86_64.whl

hint: The wheel is compatible with CPython 3.13 (`cp313d`), but you're using CPython 3.13 (`cp313`)
```

### Platform

Docker image ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:debian running on Linux 6.8.0-94-generic x86_64 GNU/Linux

### Version

0.11.2 (also reproducible with 0.10 onwards)

### Python version

Important: a DEBUG build of CPython; in this case 3.13.5

items.title: uv exclude-newer for cooldown: Stop writing timestamp in uv.lock to avoid git conflicts

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or improvement to existing functionality

items.body:
### Summary

(I've tried searching for a similar issue, and read the original issue for dependency cooldown. Didn't see a discussion of this.)

Setting a cooldown in `pyproject.toml`, like `1 week` for instance, also writes a timestamp into `uv.lock`. When upgrading a package, the timestamp gets updated.

The problem comes with larger teams working on the same code base, in multiple branches. If a package is updated in one branch, and a different package is upgraded in a separate branch, you have a merge conflict, since they both write (different) timestamps.

If `uv` _only_ wrote the span in the lock file, that would avoid merge conflicts.

Example:
```bash
git switch -c exclude-newer-base
# add exclude-newer = "1 week" to pyproject.toml
uv lock
git add -u && git commit -m "add exclude-newer cooldown"

git switch -c exclude-newer-1
uv lock -P ruff && git add -u && git commit -m "upgrade ruff"

git switch exclude-newer-base
git switch -c exclude-newer-2
uv lock -P ruff && git add -u && git commit -m "upgrade ruff"

git switch exclude-newer-base
git merge exclude-newer-1    # fast-forward
git merge exclude-newer-2    # merge conflict in uv.lock
```

items.title: `uvx run package_name` downloads and tries to run the package `run`
items.body:
### Summary

The correct command to run a tool with `uvx` is `uvx command` (i.e., `uvx ruff`). However, since `run` is used in other contexts (i.e., `uv run` inside a repository), `uvx run command` is a common typo. When the user runs `uvx run command`, uv downloads and (tries to) run the package run (which fails, since that package provides no executables). The package run is a very small, recent (first commit is from last december), and it seems safe to say that most of the times when the user runs `uvx run command` they didn't want mean the project run.

Due to `run` being used by `uv` in other contexts, `uvx run` should alert the user and ask for confirmation.

### Example

```
C:\Temp\teste>uvx --verbose run ruff
(...)
DEBUG Searching for a compatible version of run (*)
DEBUG Selecting: run==0.3 [compatible] (run-0.3-py3-none-any.whl)
(...)
```

### Platform

Windows

### Version

uvx 0.10.11 (006b56b 2026-03-16)

### Python version

Python 3.14.0
